person.note: Hazzan in Halicz between 1866-1884. A tireless scribe who copied countless prayer books and translated the Pentateuch and other books of the Bible into Karaim.
Hazzan of the Karaim community of Kukizów from ca. 1709 until his death on 17 March 1723. A scholar and a translator of biblical texts and other religious works.

The only detail we know about this individual that Zecharia ben Shalom (died 1771?) bought manuscript ADub.III.73 on the 28th of Tevet 5528, i.e. on 18 January 1768 from him. Jehuda is mentioned in the manuscript as a deceased person with the abbreviation היד, standing for Hebr. הַשֵּׁם יִקֹּם דָּמוֹ ‘may the Lord revenge his blood’, which at first sight suggests that he must have been killed in Kotov or Derazhne during the Haidamak massacre in 1768. However, the manuscript was bought in January, whereas the Haidamak rebellion broke out in spring of 1768. Ergo, Jehuda must have not necessarily been a citizen of Derazhne or Kotov.

Probably the same Zecharia ben Shalom to whom a kinah (dirge), written by Jeshua ben Mordechai Mordkowicz (chazzan in Halych until 1796) on 13 Sivan 5531 A.M. (i.e. 26 May 1771), was dedicated. The father of Mordechai ben Zecharia and Shalom ben Zacharia.

The son of Zecharia ben Shalom (?–1771?), to whom a kinah (dirge), written by Jeshua ben Mordechai Mordkowicz (chazzan in Halych until 1796) on 13 Sivan 5531 A.M. (i.e. 26 May 1771), was dedicated. The brother of Shalom ben Zecharia.

The son of Zecharia ben Shalom (?–1771?), to whom a kinah (dirge), written by Jeshua ben Mordechai Mordkowicz (chazzan in Halych until 1796) on 13 Sivan 5531 A.M. (i.e. 26 May 1771), was dedicated. The brother of Mordechai ben Zecharia.
Polish Turkologist and Orientalist of Karaim nationality, also activist of this community.

A Karaim-born scholar, Arabist and expert in Karaim studies. Community leader based in Poland, with family roots in Trakai, Lithuania. Deputy Chair of the Karaim Religious Association of Poland, the Treasurer of the Association of Polish Karaims, and Chair of the Board of the Karaim Heritage Foundation. The son of the Polish Turkologist, Dr. Aleksander Dubiński (1924–2002).
A Karaim from Halych, daughter of Shalom Szulimowicz (1808?–1886) and Channa Szulimowicz de domo Leonowicz (1823–1889). She earned the title of ha-toranit (learned in the Torah).

A Karaim from Lutsk. From 1831, he worked as a merchant of the third guild in Lutsk. He completed copying manuscript JSul.I.04 on the 15th day of Iyar 5574 A.M. (i.e. 5 May 1814 A.D.). His father, Icchak (died before 1816), served as gabbai and treasurer in the Karaim community of Lutsk.

Polish military officer and Turkologist of Karaim origin, colonel of the Armed Forces of the Polish People’s Republic, director of the Central Military Library in years 1960–1972. Bibliophile, collector of Karaim manuscripts.

Polish Turkologist, expert in Karaim studies, doctor of theology, renowned literary translator. Researcher at the University of Warsaw (Poland). Vice-chair of the Association of Polish Karaims. The daughter of the Polish Turkologist Józef Sulimowicz (1913–1973).

A descendant of Crimean Karaims. His father, Jakow Markowicz Kokenaj, was a teacher at a Karaim school. He completed five years of gymnasium in Feodosia but, due to illness, was unable to continue his education. A self-taught scholar, he became a distinguished expert on Karaim history. He authored a Karaim–Russian dictionary and assembled a significant collection of books on Karaim studies.

A Karaim of Halych, married to Malka ha-toranit (learned in the Torah). Member of the Leonowicz family. Son of Levi ben Jeshua ha-Rosh, an elder of the community. Brother of Abraham ha-Shofet Leonowicz (1776–1851), who was the hazzan of the Karaim community in Halych in the years 1802 (1810)–1851.

Arabist, Turkologist, Iranist, expert in the field of Philology of the Islamic East. The founder of modern Polish Oriental Studies. Worked to establish institutional frameworks for Oriental Studies in the newly reborn Poland. Studied in Vienna (1907–1911; he earned his Ph.D. there), Strasbourg, and Kiel (1911–1912). Habilitation in Arabic studies in Kraków (1914), Professor at the Jagiellonian University in Kraków from 1919, Secretary General of the Polish Academy of Learning. Worked to establish institutional frameworks for Oriental Studies in the newly reborn Poland – through university cooperation ministerial lobbying. Arrested by the Nazis during Sonderaktion Krakau and was imprisoned in the Sachsenhausen concentration camp until his liberation in February 1940. Died in 1948, in the age of 59, due to worsened health condition.
Polish ethnographer, the daughter of Prof. Dr. Tadeusz Jan Kowalski (1889–1948), the founder of modern Polish Oriental Studies.

Arabist at the Jagiellonian University in Kraków. The daughter of Dr. Anna Kowalska-Lewicka (1920–2009), an ethnographer, and Prof. Dr. Tadeusz Lewicki (1906–1992), orientalist, Arabist, and medieval historian.

A speaker of Northwest Karaim. He was a prolific copyist with extensive training in calligraphy; one of the few to prepare a copy of the entire Tanakh. He was elected hazzan in Panevėžys, probably in the mid-1890s.

Karaim clergyman, writer, and poet (pen name Szafir) based in the Vilnius region. From 1920 to 1982, he served as a clergyman at the Trakai kenesa (elected hazzan on 20 September 1920; in 1922–1928 he was acting hacham, and from 1929 he served as ullu hazzan).
